summary: BBN's host status report for January 17 to 28, 1972, noting that the Utah and Rand PDP-10 hosts became servers. It was replaced by RFC 306.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 298 records ARPANET host status from January 17 through January 28, 1972. Its tables show daily test results and note that the Utah and Rand PDP-10s became network servers.

subtitle: A report on ARPANET host status from January 17 to January 28, 1972.

tldr.problem: ARPANET users and operators needed a record of which network hosts were accessible and available as servers.
tldr.mechanism: The report lists daily host test results, host status or predictions, and categories of hosts excluded from daily testing.
tldr.outcome: RFC 298 is an early host status report and was obsoleted by RFC 306.

today: RFC 298 is an early host status report and has been obsoleted by RFC 306.

sections.title: The Reporting Period
sections.content:
RFC 298 reports the status of most Network Hosts from January 17 to January 28. It notes that the Utah PDP-10 and Rand PDP-10 became Network servers during that period.

The report excludes hosts not expected to function as servers regularly for at least two weeks and hosts intended only as users. It then presents tables of host tests and status or predictions.
sections.plainLanguage: This report shows which ARPANET hosts answered tests during a two-week period. It also records that the Utah and Rand PDP-10s became servers.

sections.title: Daily Test Results
sections.content:
The report gives test results for January 17-21 and January 24-28, with a site address, site, computer, and a status for each test. The status codes are O for Open, D for Dead, H for Half Open, R for Refused, and T for Timed out.

A timeout means the host did not complete connection establishment and open a connection within 60 seconds. A hash mark indicates that a site had warned that its system might not be available at that time.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables record whether each host opened a connection, failed, refused, or timed out. A timeout means the connection did not open within 60 seconds.

sections.title: Host Roles and Availability Notes
sections.content:
A separate table lists each site's status or prediction, such as server, user only, or a date when a host was expected to become available. The report marks the Network Control Center as a statistics-gathering host and lists Terminal IMPs as user-only hosts.

The RFC also notes that the UCLA IBM-360/91 offered the Network Job Service, which the BBN Terminal IMP could not test. The report assumes an initial connection to its logger indicated that service was functioning.
sections.plainLanguage: The report distinguishes hosts that offered services from user-only hosts. It also explains that one listed service could not be checked by the test equipment.

references.text: Westheimer, E., "Network Host Status", RFC 267, November 1971.
